A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same nationality-persona study, with matching authors, datasets, and central questions. All text, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: V1 reports original LLM-response experiments, regional RP/PMR measurements, persona-sensitivity statistics, and comparisons between elicited model responses and published human surveys.

after.justification: V2 reports original model-response measurements under revised prompting and model settings, including country case studies and comparisons of adjective-based and survey-question elicitation.

M1.justification: Persona elicitation expands from the single identity-instruction pattern in v1 Table 1 to three adopted persona templates in v2 Table 1. This modestly adapts the prompting procedure while retaining the central nationality-persona and adjective-elicitation approach; no new model architecture or training method is proposed.

E1.justification: Both versions use 193 nationalities, the same 516-adjective English collection, five regional groups, and the same country/persona sets from Pew and Gallup surveys. V2's country case studies analyze subsets of existing coverage rather than introducing new populations or tasks.

E2.justification: The evaluated model comparison suite replaces Llama-2-13B and Gemma-7B with Llama-3.1-70B and Gemma2-27B; Appendix B also changes Mistral from v0.1 to v0.3. These changes appear throughout the reported comparisons. V2 Tables 4–5 additionally compare adjective-based and direct-survey elicitation, previously analyzed separately.

E3.justification: V2 averages results across three prompting templates rather than one instruction pattern and evaluates revised model configurations. Section 4 changes the response taxonomy from eight categories to seven, dropping Multiple Regions. The added country case studies also introduce a minimum of five responses per displayed country.

E4.justification: V2 adds country-frequency analyses, American/Russian/Indian/Chinese persona case studies, and direct validation of adjective-based PMR against human survey judgments (Sections 5.3–5.6). These investigate diversity, geopolitical associations, and measurement validity beyond v1's analyses. V1 Figure 3/Table 7's complete persona-region matrix is not retained.

E5.justification: V1 Appendix D specifies 100 survey repetitions at default temperature plus 100 at 1.25. V2 Section 5.6 reports 100 repetitions per country/model within its three-template design, without clarifying allocation across templates. This changes repetition reporting without establishing a definite reduction in total runs. Chi-squared testing remains unchanged, and neither version reports confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Main and appendix results are extensively replaced under revised settings. For example, Table 3's Mistral correlation for other nations' views of the U.S. changes from -0.23 to 0.57. The most persona-sensitive evaluated model changes from Gemma-7B to Mistral-7B. Numerous country-level and elicitation-comparison results are added; these are not same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: The RP, PMR, normalized Kendall-distance, and survey-comparison concepts remain unchanged. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs. V2's expanded account of representational bias is conceptual interpretation rather than a new mathematical definition.

C1.justification: V1's headline finding says personas correlate with U.S. survey responses but not other countries' responses. V2 broadens this to correlations with corresponding nations' surveys, qualified by poor absolute agreement and strongest U.S. alignment, and adds this finding to the abstract. The central Western-bias and persona-focus claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly grounds bias in representational harm, interprets country associations through geopolitical conflicts, and qualifies own-region positivity using country case studies. It also explains differences between direct-survey and adjective-based estimates through positivity bias and ranking-versus-absolute agreement. The two existing limitations paragraphs remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 adds country-extraction priority, refusal keywords, invalid-response examples, annotator background, fuller task prompts, and a P2-dataset disclosure. Model frameworks and quantization details are updated. However, v1's survey-temperature instructions disappear. The code/data repository link remains unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds Blodgett et al. (2020) to ground representational-harm framing and Kamruzzaman et al. (2024) for response extraction. It newly attributes its three prompting templates to the already-cited Gupta et al. (2023). The main related-work discussion otherwise remains substantially the same.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially reframed around representational harm and three explicit research questions. Results are reorganized into six thematic subsections with prominent finding statements, and terminology shifts toward generated evaluations rather than anthropomorphic perceptions. Survey instructions move from an appendix table into Section 5.6.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the regional heatmap presentation with multiple country and region bar-chart panels, changes the map from regional to country-level polarity, and adds case-study figures. Prompt and result tables are restructured, new elicitation-comparison tables appear, and the complete regional matrix is removed. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: V2 improves conceptual framing and extraction documentation and adds useful country analyses and PMR-versus-survey validation. However, survey-temperature details disappear and important numerical discrepancies remain unexplained: Figure 6(a) places American-persona U.K. PMR above 50%, while Table 5 reports 8.33%; Table 2's seven Mistral response percentages total only 96.90%. These issues limit confidence in the expanded evidence, making the net overall quality change uncertain.
